p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between a warehouse and a distribution center?
t: A warehouse is designed mainly to store goods; a distribution center is designed to move them quickly. Distribution centers usually have more dock doors, deeper truck courts, more trailer parking, and more employees and conveyors, because inventory turns over in days rather than months. Many buildings can serve either use. The dock count, truck court, and parking decide which.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Flex space is an industrial building with a high share of finished office or showroom area (often a quarter or more of the building) combined with warehouse, lab, or light assembly space behind it. It usually has lower clear heights and more grade-level or drive-in doors than a warehouse. Flex suits companies that need offices and goods under one roof. See flex space in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Small-bay (or shallow-bay) industrial is a building divided into small suites, often from a few thousand to roughly 25,000 square feet each, leased to contractors, service businesses, distributors, and light manufacturers. Suites typically have a small office, a drive-in or dock door, and their own utilities. Small-bay buildings in the 10,000 to 100,000 SF range are a deep, local market because few new ones are built.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a last-mile industrial facility?
t: A last-mile (or last-touch) facility is a warehouse or service building close to dense population, used for the final leg of delivery to homes and businesses. Location matters more than size or height: proximity to customers, labor, and arterial roads, plus parking for vans and fleet vehicles. Infill sites near Chicago and inner-ring suburbs are classic last-mile locations.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Industrial outdoor storage is land used to park trucks and trailers, stage equipment, or store materials. It is usually paved or gravel, fenced, and lit, with little or no building. Value depends on zoning that permits outdoor storage, access, surfacing, stormwater compliance, and scarcity, because many municipalities restrict new outdoor storage. See IOS in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is cold storage, and why is it different?
t: Cold storage is a temperature-controlled warehouse for refrigerated or frozen goods. Insulated panels, refrigeration systems, freezer-grade floors with under-slab heating, heavy power, and specialized docks make it far more expensive to build and convert than a dry warehouse. That cost, plus food-safety requirements, keeps supply limited and tenants sticky.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do Class A, B, and C mean for industrial buildings?
t: Building class is shorthand for age and functionality. Class A buildings are newer with modern clear heights, ESFR sprinklers, deep truck courts, and wide column spacing. Class B buildings are older but functional. Class C buildings have significant limitations such as low clear height, tight columns, or poor access. Class is not a universal standard. Always compare actual specifications. See industrial building classes .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who leases and owns industrial buildings?
t: Tenants include manufacturers, distributors, third-party logistics (3PL) providers, e-commerce and retail companies, contractors, food and beverage firms, and service businesses. Owners range from owner-users who occupy their buildings to private investors, family offices, syndicators, private equity funds, institutional investors, and publicly traded REITs. In the 10,000 to 100,000 SF range, owner-users and private investors are the most common buyers.

t: What is clear height in a warehouse? Clear height is the usable vertical distance from the floor to the lowest overhead obstruction, usually the bottom of the roof joists, beams, or sprinkler lines. It sets how high goods can be racked, which drives storage capacity per square foot. Measure it at the lowest point, not at the roof peak. See clear height in the glossary . How much clear height does a modern warehouse need? Modern bulk distribution buildings are commonly built with clear heights in the mid-30s to 40 feet, while many functional small-bay and older buildings have roughly 16 to 24 feet. The right height depends on the user: racked distribution benefits from height, but contractors, service users, and light manufacturers often value doors, power, and yard more. Match the building to its realistic tenant pool. What is the difference between dock-high and grade-level doors? A dock-high door sits at truck-bed height, roughly four feet above the truck court, so forklifts can drive directly into semi-trailers. A grade-level (drive-in) door sits at ground level so vehicles and equipment can drive into the building. Distribution users need docks; contractors and service users often need drive-in doors. p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How many dock doors does a warehouse need?
t: It depends on throughput. A frequently cited rule of thumb for distribution is about one dock door per 5,000 to 10,000 square feet, with fast-moving cross-dock or parcel operations needing more and long-term storage needing fewer. Count usable doors with working levelers, seals, and trailer positions, not just openings in the wall.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a truck court, and how deep should it be?
t: The truck court is the paved area in front of the dock doors where tractor-trailers maneuver and park. Depth is critical: modern facilities commonly provide roughly 120 to 135 feet for a single-sided court and more when trucks share a court from both sides. A shallow court limits which trucks can use the building and is one of the hardest features to fix. See truck court . Those depths are screening examples, not a safe-clearance guarantee. Review the sourced vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference , then have a qualified engineer check the actual fleet's entry, backing, and exit paths.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Why does column spacing matter in an industrial building?
t: Column spacing, the distance between interior roof-support columns, determines how efficiently racking, aisles, and equipment fit. Wider spacing gives more layout flexibility; tight spacing wastes floor area and can rule out some users. Modern buildings commonly use bays around 50 feet wide with deeper speed bays at the docks. See column spacing .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an ESFR sprinkler system?
t: ESFR (early suppression, fast response) is a ceiling-level sprinkler system designed to suppress high-piled storage fires without in-rack sprinklers in many configurations. Whether a system is adequate depends on the commodity, storage height, building height, and water supply, so a system that works for one tenant may not work for the next. A fire-protection engineer should confirm it. See ESFR sprinklers .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much electrical power does an industrial building need?
t: Warehouses with lighting and battery charging may need modest service, while manufacturing, cold storage, and EV-fleet users can require far more. Industrial service is usually described by amperage, voltage, and phase. Three-phase power is standard for motors and machinery. Confirm actual service with an electrician and the utility, because upgrades can take months. See three-phase power .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I know about the floor slab?
t: The slab carries racking, forklifts, and machinery, so its thickness, reinforcement, load capacity, and flatness matter. Tall racking and narrow-aisle equipment need flat, level floors; heavy manufacturing needs high load capacity. Ask for original drawings, look for cracking or joint failure, and have an engineer evaluate the slab for demanding uses. See slab load and flatness .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much office space is typical in an industrial building?
t: Warehouse and distribution buildings often have a small office share (commonly under 10 to 15 percent of the building), while flex buildings may have far more. More office is not always better: excess office raises operating costs, may sit empty, and narrows the tenant pool. Compare office percentage with what local users actually need. See office finish percentage .

t: How do industrial leases usually work? Most industrial leases are net leases: the tenant pays base rent plus its share of property taxes, insurance, and common-area or maintenance costs. Terms set the rent schedule, length, permitted use, repair responsibilities, renewal options, and what happens at move-out. Because terms vary widely, compare total occupancy cost rather than base rent alone. The lease comparison guide explains how. What is a triple-net (NNN) lease? A triple-net lease requires the tenant to pay base rent plus its share of the three “nets”: real estate taxes, building insurance, and common-area maintenance. It is the most common structure for industrial property. Leases called NNN still differ on who replaces the roof, structure, parking lot, and HVAC, so read the repair and capital clauses. t: CAM (common area maintenance) charges are a tenant’s share of costs to operate and maintain shared parts of a property, such as snow removal, landscaping, parking-lot repair, lighting, and sometimes management fees. Ask what is included, how shares are calculated, whether there are caps, and whether capital replacements can be passed through. See CAM in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Industrial leases are commonly three to ten years. Small-bay and small-business tenants often sign three- to five-year terms, while large distribution and build-to-suit leases can run ten years or longer. Longer terms usually come with more landlord-funded improvements and free rent; shorter terms keep the tenant flexible. Renewal options extend the term at the tenant’s choice.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do rent escalations work in industrial leases?
t: Most industrial leases increase base rent each year by a fixed percentage or a fixed dollar amount per square foot; some use CPI-based or stepped increases. The rate negotiated reflects market conditions at signing. Escalations compound over the term, so model total rent over the full lease. See escalations .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a tenant improvement (TI) allowance?
t: A TI allowance is money the landlord contributes toward building out or modifying the tenant’s space, such as offices, electrical, lighting, restrooms, or dock work. It is usually expressed per square foot and is tied to lease term and credit; the landlord recovers it through rent. Clarify who manages construction and what happens to unused allowance. See TI allowance .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Industrial rent is usually quoted in dollars per square foot per year on a net basis, with estimated taxes, insurance, and CAM listed separately. Smaller suites are sometimes quoted as a monthly gross amount. Always ask whether a number is net or gross, annual or monthly, and what the current operating-expense estimate is.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays for the roof, HVAC, and structural repairs in an industrial lease?
t: It depends on the lease. Commonly, tenants handle routine repairs and maintenance of their space and HVAC, while landlords keep responsibility for roof replacement and structure. However, some “absolute NNN” leases shift everything to the tenant. Read who repairs and who replaces, and whether replacement costs can be amortized into CAM.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I ask before leasing a warehouse?
t: Confirm zoning allows your use; clear height, door types and count, truck-court depth, and trailer parking; electrical service; sprinkler adequacy for your storage; office and restroom count; current taxes, insurance, and CAM; repair and replacement responsibilities; renewal and expansion rights; restoration obligations at move-out; and access hours, security, and outdoor storage rights. The tour checklist covers what to measure.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Should a business lease or buy its industrial building?
t: Buying offers control, equity build-up, protection from rent increases, and a long-term asset, at the cost of capital, concentration risk, and responsibility for repairs. Leasing preserves cash and flexibility to grow or move. Companies with stable, long-term needs and specialized improvements often buy, sometimes with SBA 504 financing; fast-growing companies often lease. Compare both over the same time horizon with your accountant.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: A build-to-suit is a building designed and built for a specific tenant or buyer, usually committed before construction starts. The user gets exactly the specifications it needs in exchange for a long lease or purchase commitment; the developer gets reduced leasing risk. Lead times include site selection, entitlements, design, and construction, which together often take a year or more.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a speculative (spec) industrial building?
t: A spec building is constructed without a signed tenant, on the developer’s expectation that demand will lease it. Spec buildings are usually designed to generic modern standards so they fit many users. They let tenants move faster than a build-to-suit, and they add competitive supply that affects rents in a submarket.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an industrial sublease, and is it a good option?
t: A sublease is a lease from an existing tenant to a new occupant for some or all of the tenant’s space, usually requiring landlord consent. Subleases can be cheaper and faster, often with furniture or racking in place, but the term is limited to the remaining original lease and the subtenant depends on the original tenant staying in good standing. Read the master lease.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What security deposit or guaranty will an industrial landlord ask for?
t: Landlords size security to the risk: tenant financials, time in business, lease length, and how much the landlord is spending on improvements and commissions. Expect a cash deposit or letter of credit, and for smaller or newer companies, a personal or corporate guaranty. Negotiate burn-downs that reduce security after a period of on-time payment.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays the broker on an industrial lease?
t: In most commercial leases the landlord pays leasing commissions under its listing agreement, and a tenant’s broker is typically paid from that commission. Arrangements vary, so ask how each broker is compensated and confirm any agency disclosures Illinois requires. See leasing commission .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a letter of intent (LOI) in commercial real estate?
t: A letter of intent summarizes the main business terms (price or rent, term, contingencies, timing, and key conditions) before lawyers draft the purchase agreement or lease. LOIs are usually non-binding on business terms, though confidentiality or exclusivity provisions may be binding. A clear LOI prevents surprises in the final documents. See LOI .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Is industrial real estate a good investment? Industrial has been one of the stronger commercial property types over the past decade, supported by e-commerce, supply-chain restructuring, and limited new supply in infill areas. Buildings are relatively simple to operate and often leased net. But returns depend on the price paid, rents, lease terms, interest rates, and new construction. No property type is a good investment at any price. The investment guide explains how to evaluate one. What are the advantages of investing in industrial property? p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do I start investing in industrial real estate?
t: Options range from buying public industrial REIT shares, to investing passively in a syndication or fund, to buying a building directly. Direct buyers often start with a smaller single-tenant or small-bay building in a market they know, assemble a team (broker, attorney, lender, inspector, environmental consultant, accountant), and learn to read leases and operating statements before making offers.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: An industrial REIT (real estate investment trust) is a company that owns and usually operates industrial properties and distributes most of its taxable income to shareholders. Public REITs offer liquidity and diversification but no control over individual buildings, and their share prices move with the stock market. Direct ownership offers control and tax planning options but less liquidity.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do core, value-add, and opportunistic mean?
t: They describe risk strategies. Core is stabilized, well-located property with long leases and low leverage. Core-plus adds modest upside. Value-add involves leasing up vacancy, renovating, or re-tenanting to raise income. Opportunistic includes development, heavy repositioning, or distressed situations with the highest risk and expected return. See value-add vs. core .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between an owner-user and an investor buyer?
t: An owner-user buys a building to occupy it, valuing location, layout, and control; an investor buys for the income from tenants. Owner-users can sometimes pay more for a vacant or soon-to-be-vacant building, especially with SBA 504 financing, while investors pay for leases in place. Which buyer pool fits a building affects pricing and marketing strategy. See owner-user vs. investor .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a 1031 exchange, and how does it work for industrial property?
t: A Section 1031 like-kind exchange lets an investor defer federal capital gains tax by reinvesting proceeds from a sold investment property into another investment property. Under IRS rules, replacement property must be identified within 45 days and acquired within 180 days, and proceeds are held by a qualified intermediary. Industrial can be exchanged for other real property held for investment or business use. Work with a tax advisor. See 1031 exchange .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: In a sale-leaseback, a business sells the building it occupies to an investor and simultaneously signs a long-term lease to stay. The seller converts real estate equity into working capital while keeping operations in place; the buyer gets a leased property with a known tenant. The rent and lease terms drive the price. See the selling guide’s sale-leaseback section .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you finance an industrial property purchase?
t: Common sources are banks and credit unions, life insurance companies, CMBS lenders, debt funds, and SBA 504 or 7(a) loans for owner-users. Lenders size loans by loan-to-value, debt service coverage, and sometimes debt yield, and look closely at lease term, tenant credit, and environmental reports. Compare rate, term, amortization, recourse, reserves, and prepayment terms, not just the interest rate. See financing in the investment guide .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: What is a cap rate? A capitalization rate is a property’s net operating income divided by its price or value. A building with $100,000 of NOI selling for $1.5 million has a cap rate of about 6.7 percent. Lower cap rates mean higher prices relative to income. Always confirm whether a quoted cap rate uses in-place, projected, or adjusted income. Try the cap-rate calculator . What is a good cap rate for industrial property? There is no single good cap rate. It depends on interest rates, location, building quality, lease term, tenant credit, rent relative to market, and expected capital spending. A low cap rate on a long lease to a strong tenant can be a better deal than a high cap rate on a building with near-term vacancy. Compare against recent sales of truly similar buildings and current borrowing costs. How is an industrial property valued? Appraisers and buyers use three approaches. The income approach capitalizes or discounts net operating income and usually leads for leased investment property. The sales comparison approach compares recent sales of similar buildings and often leads for owner-user property. The cost approach estimates land plus depreciated replacement cost and serves as a check. See how buyers underwrite . What is net operating income (NOI)? t: There is no single good cap rate. It depends on interest rates, location, building quality, lease term, tenant credit, rent relative to market, and expected capital spending. A low cap rate on a long lease to a strong tenant can be a better deal than a high cap rate on a building with near-term vacancy. Compare against recent sales of truly similar buildings and current borrowing costs.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How is an industrial property valued?
t: Appraisers and buyers use three approaches. The income approach capitalizes or discounts net operating income and usually leads for leased investment property. The sales comparison approach compares recent sales of similar buildings and often leads for owner-user property. The cost approach estimates land plus depreciated replacement cost and serves as a check. See how buyers underwrite .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: Net operating income is a property’s rental and other income minus operating expenses such as taxes, insurance, repairs, utilities, and management, before debt payments, depreciation, income taxes, and usually capital reserves. In net leases most expenses are reimbursed, so NOI is close to base rent minus unrecovered costs. See NOI .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How useful is price per square foot for industrial property?
t: Price per square foot is a quick comparison tool, especially for owner-user and vacant buildings, but it hides differences in land, clear height, office finish, yard, condition, and lease terms. Use it alongside income-based value and replacement cost, and compare only truly similar buildings in the same submarket and size range.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is WALT, and why does it matter?
t: WALT (weighted average lease term) is the average remaining lease term across a property’s tenants, weighted by rent or square footage. Longer WALT means more predictable income and easier financing; shorter WALT means more rollover risk, but also more opportunity to reset rents to market. See WALT .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) is NOI divided by annual loan payments; lenders commonly want a cushion above 1.0, often around 1.25 or higher. LTV (loan-to-value) is the loan amount divided by the property’s value. The lower of the two tests usually sets the maximum loan. See DSCR and LTV .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are IRR, equity multiple, and cash-on-cash return?
t: Cash-on-cash return is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by equity invested. Equity multiple is total cash returned divided by equity invested over the hold. IRR is the annualized return that accounts for the timing of every cash flow, including sale proceeds. Each answers a different question, so investors look at all three. See IRR .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you determine market rent for an industrial building?
t: Market rent comes from recently signed leases for comparable space (similar size, location, clear height, doors, office finish, and condition), adjusted for concessions such as free rent and improvement allowances. Asking rents and listings show landlord expectations, not signed deals. Brokers and appraisers track lease comparables; ask for them.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do interest rates affect industrial property values?
t: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and investors’ required returns, which tends to push cap rates up and prices down unless rents grow enough to offset it. Lower rates generally do the opposite. The effect is not one-for-one: rent growth, supply, and investor demand also matter. Model financing at realistic rates, not the lowest available.

h: What documents do I need to sell an industrial property?
t: Typical files include leases and amendments, a rent roll, two to three years of operating statements, tax bills and any appeal history, service contracts, a title policy, survey, prior environmental and property condition reports, permits and certificates of occupancy, roof and equipment warranties, utility information, and site plans. p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Is it better to sell an industrial building vacant or leased?
t: It depends on who will pay more. A vacant building appeals to owner-users, who may pay a premium for a functional building in the right location. A leased building appeals to investors, who pay for the income. Long, market-rate leases usually command the strongest investor pricing. Short or below-market leases can reduce value to both pools.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What does an industrial investment sales broker do?
t: An investment sales broker prices the property, prepares marketing materials, identifies and qualifies buyers, manages tours and confidentiality, runs the offer process, negotiates terms, and keeps diligence and closing on schedule. Commissions are usually a percentage of the sale price paid by the seller at closing under a listing agreement. Choose a broker with recent experience selling similar buildings in your submarket.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Should I sell off-market or with a full marketing process?
t: A full marketing process exposes the property to more buyers and usually produces the most competitive price. An off-market sale offers privacy, less disruption to tenants, and speed, but may leave money on the table. A targeted process to a short list of qualified buyers is a middle path. See confidentiality and marketing .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What taxes apply when I sell an industrial building?
t: Federal capital gains tax generally applies to the gain, and depreciation taken is recaptured. For real property, unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is taxed at a federal rate of up to 25 percent. Illinois income tax and, in some cases, the net investment income tax may also apply, and state, county, and local transfer taxes are due at closing. A 1031 exchange can defer gain. Plan with a tax advisor before you list.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What happens after I accept an offer on my industrial property?
t: The parties sign a purchase and sale agreement, the buyer deposits earnest money, and a due diligence period begins for inspections, environmental review, title and survey, lease review, and estoppels. After diligence, the deposit typically becomes non-refundable except for specified conditions, the buyer finalizes financing, and the sale closes. See PSA and earnest money .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do I prepare my industrial building for sale?
t: Organize documents, resolve deferred maintenance that buyers will price aggressively (roof leaks, dock equipment, pavement, life safety), clean up the yard, confirm permits and zoning compliance, address known environmental questions, and line up tenant renewals where possible. See physical preparation .

h: What is a Phase II environmental assessment?
t: A Phase II is sampling of soil, groundwater, soil vapor, or building materials to test whether conditions flagged in a Phase I have actually caused contamination and how much. It is common at sites with historic manufacturing, underground tanks, dry cleaning, or chemical use. Results can lead to remediation, price adjustments, insurance, or a decision not to buy.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are common environmental issues at industrial sites?
t: Frequent issues include leaking underground or aboveground storage tanks, chlorinated solvents from degreasing, petroleum, metals, PCBs in older equipment, asbestos and lead in building materials, vapor intrusion, fill material of unknown origin, and emerging contaminants such as PFAS. Adjacent properties can also contaminate a site through groundwater.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a property condition assessment?
t: A property condition assessment is an engineer’s review of a building’s roof, structure, paving, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire protection, and accessibility, with estimated repair costs and a replacement schedule. For industrial buildings, pay special attention to roof age, dock equipment, slab, sprinklers, and truck-court pavement. See physical diligence .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an ALTA survey, and why do lenders want one?
t: An ALTA/NSPS land title survey maps boundaries, easements, encroachments, improvements, access, and flood zone to national standards so a title insurer can remove the standard survey exception. Lenders typically require one. For industrial sites it confirms truck access, parking, rail spurs, and whether buildings or fences cross property lines. See ALTA survey .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What does a title commitment show, and what does title insurance cover?
t: A title commitment lists the current owner, legal description, liens, easements, restrictions, and requirements to close. Title insurance protects the buyer and lender against covered defects in title that were not excluded, such as forged documents or undisclosed liens. Review every exception. Easements and recorded restrictions can limit how an industrial site is used. See title commitment .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a tenant estoppel certificate?
t: An estoppel certificate is a signed statement from a tenant confirming key lease facts: rent, term, deposits, options, amendments, and whether either party is in default. Buyers and lenders rely on estoppels to confirm that the leases match what the seller represented. See estoppel certificate .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an Illinois No Further Remediation (NFR) letter?
t: An NFR letter is issued by the Illinois EPA, typically through its Site Remediation Program or leaking UST program, after a site meets cleanup objectives for a defined use. It often includes land-use restrictions or engineered barriers that must be maintained and recorded. Read the conditions before assuming a site is “clean” for every use.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
t: What zoning does a warehouse or industrial use need? Industrial uses generally need a manufacturing or industrial zoning district, and each municipality defines which uses are permitted, which need a special use, and which are prohibited. Outdoor storage, truck terminals, and heavy manufacturing are often restricted. In unincorporated areas the county zoning ordinance applies. Get the zoning designation and a written confirmation of your use from the local authority. What is a Planned Manufacturing District (PMD) in Chicago? A Planned Manufacturing District is a Chicago zoning designation created to protect concentrations of industrial businesses from conversion to residential and other non-industrial uses. PMDs restrict incompatible uses within their boundaries. Check the City of Chicago zoning map for whether a property is in a PMD and what that permits. See the Chicago research guide . What are Chicago’s industrial corridors? Chicago’s industrial corridors are city-designated areas with concentrated industrial land and businesses, used to guide land-use policy and economic-development programs. p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between a special use and a variance?
t: A special use (sometimes called a conditional use) is a use the zoning code allows only after a public review that can impose conditions. A variance is relief from a specific standard, such as setbacks, parking, or height, when strict application would cause hardship. Both require applications and hearings, so build time into any plan that depends on them. See special use and variance .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is different about industrial property in unincorporated areas?
t: Property outside a municipality is governed by the county for zoning, building permits, and often water, sewer, and police services. That can mean different rules and costs than a neighboring village, and future annexation can change both. Confirm jurisdiction before relying on any zoning or utility assumption. See unincorporated vs. incorporated .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How are industrial property taxes calculated in Illinois?
t: The assessor estimates market value and applies an assessment level to get assessed value; a state or county equalization factor may then apply; exemptions are subtracted; and the result is multiplied by the combined rate of every local taxing district. Rates are set by those districts’ levies, not by the assessor. See the property tax guide .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Why are Cook County industrial property taxes different from the collar counties?
t: Cook County classifies property and assesses industrial property at 25 percent of market value, reassesses by region on a three-year cycle, and applies a state equalizer. The other counties generally assess at the statewide standard of one-third of market value with township assessors and annual equalization. Tax rates differ by district too. See Cook vs. collar counties .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the Cook County Class 6b incentive?
t: Class 6b is a Cook County incentive that reduces the assessment level for qualifying industrial property that is newly built, substantially rehabilitated, or reoccupied after vacancy. The reduced level is commonly 10 percent of market value for ten years, then 15 and 20 percent in the final two years, compared with the standard 25 percent. It requires municipal support and timely application. Confirm current rules with the Cook County Assessor. See Cook County incentives .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do I appeal industrial property taxes in Illinois?
t: In Cook County you can appeal to the Assessor during your township’s window and then to the Board of Review; in other counties you appeal to the county Board of Review. Further appeals can go to the state Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court. Deadlines are short, and evidence such as income, comparable sales, vacancy, or an appraisal matters. See appeals and deadlines .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays real estate transfer tax in Illinois?
t: Illinois imposes a state transfer tax, counties impose a county tax, and some municipalities, including Chicago, add their own. By custom the seller usually pays the state and county taxes, but municipal ordinances decide who pays the local tax, and Chicago’s tax falls largely on the buyer. Rates and exemptions change, so confirm with your attorney and the municipality before closing. See transfer tax .

h: What is the industrial vacancy rate in Chicago?
t: Chicago’s industrial vacancy rate changes quarterly and differs by submarket, building size, and age. Large new distribution buildings and small infill buildings can move in opposite directions. Check the latest quarterly market reports from major brokerages and compare the same definitions over time. The daily industrial news on the home page links recent coverage.

h: Are Chicago industrial rents going up?
t: Over the past several years Chicago industrial rents rose with strong demand, while the pace has varied by submarket and with new speculative supply. Small-bay and infill rents often behave differently from big-box rents. For current direction, rely on recent signed lease comparables in your submarket and size range rather than regional averages.

h: Which Chicagoland county is best for industrial property?

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: What does “below-market rent” really mean, and how do I underwrite the mark-to-market?
t: Only signed, comparable leases establish market rent, and in small-bay buildings the comparable set is narrow: suite size, office finish, door type, power, and yard rights all move the number. Treat broker asking rents as asking rents. Then remember that rent only resets when a lease expires. Model each expiration with a retention probability, months of downtime, improvement costs, commissions, and any free rent. Do not pay for the upside in the price and count it again in the pro forma.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: How should I set the exit cap rate and hold period?
t: The exit cap rate is usually the most sensitive assumption in the model, and the building will be older at exit than it is today. Many disciplined buyers refuse to assume an exit cap below the going-in rate without a specific reason such as a longer lease or a completed renovation. Run sensitivities rather than a single case: a higher exit cap, lower market rent, longer downtime, and a delayed sale. If the deal only works in the base case, the base case is doing too much work.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
t: Does clear height matter for buildings this size, or only for bulk distribution? It matters relative to the tenant pool. Service companies, contractors, light assembly, and last-mile operators in 10,000 to 40,000 SF spaces often care more about drive-in doors, power, office ratio, parking, and yard than about an extra few feet of clearance. Distribution users and third-party logistics tenants care about dock count, truck court, and racking height. Buy for the users who will realistically lease the space, and underwrite rents for that pool. The building-fit checklist walks through what to measure on a tour. What makes a Class B or C building “functionally obsolete,” and can capital fix it? Some things capital fixes: roof, lighting, dock equipment, pavement, office refresh, electrical service, and sometimes adding dock positions. Some it cannot: low clear height, tight column spacing, a shallow truck court, high site coverage with no expansion land, and poor access. Those permanent features cap the rent the building can earn and narrow the future buyer pool. h: Does clear height matter for buildings this size, or only for bulk distribution?
t: It matters relative to the tenant pool. Service companies, contractors, light assembly, and last-mile operators in 10,000 to 40,000 SF spaces often care more about drive-in doors, power, office ratio, parking, and yard than about an extra few feet of clearance. Distribution users and third-party logistics tenants care about dock count, truck court, and racking height. Buy for the users who will realistically lease the space, and underwrite rents for that pool. The building-fit checklist walks through what to measure on a tour.

h: What makes a Class B or C building “functionally obsolete,” and can capital fix it?
t: Some things capital fixes: roof, lighting, dock equipment, pavement, office refresh, electrical service, and sometimes adding dock positions. Some it cannot: low clear height, tight column spacing, a shallow truck court, high site coverage with no expansion land, and poor access. Those permanent features cap the rent the building can earn and narrow the future buyer pool. Price the permanent limitations rather than planning around them, and keep in mind that a well-located, functional Class B building serving local demand can be a durable asset precisely because nobody builds its replacement.

h: How do I value excess land or an outdoor storage yard attached to a building?
t: Start with permission, not price. Confirm that the zoning and any approvals allow outdoor storage, trailer parking, or equipment staging; many municipalities restrict them even in industrial districts. Then verify legal access, surfacing, lighting, drainage and stormwater compliance, and whether the yard can be leased separately from the building. Yard income with clear permission and separate leaseability is worth more than yard that is merely tolerated. The nine-county hub links the zoning authorities to ask.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: Multi-tenant or single-tenant: which is less risky in this size range?
t: Multi-tenant buildings spread vacancy risk across several leases but bring more frequent rollover, demising and metering questions, and hands-on management. Single-tenant buildings are simpler to own and finance but carry binary vacancy risk and depend on one company’s health. The better question is which risk you are equipped to manage. If you cannot lease and manage small suites efficiently, diversification on paper becomes vacancy in practice.

h: How do I underwrite rollover and downtime realistically?
t: Build the model lease by lease rather than with a blended vacancy factor. For each expiration assign a retention probability, months of downtime if the tenant leaves, improvement and commission costs, and free rent. Then stress the schedule: two tenants leaving in the same year, a renewal at a lower rent, a longer lease-up. Where rollover is concentrated, consider negotiating early renewals or extensions before closing. Sellers often prefer certainty too.

h: In a sale-leaseback, what am I really buying?
t: Two things: the seller-tenant’s ability to pay rent for the lease term, and the real estate you would own if it stopped. The rent is often set by the seller’s financing need, not by the market, so test it against market rent to see how much residual risk sits in the building itself. Lease term, guaranties, financial-reporting covenants, and maintenance obligations deserve the same attention as price. The selling guide explains the structure from the owner-user’s side.

h: If the building is already operating, how much does zoning conformity matter?
t: A lot, if you ever want to change the use, expand, add outdoor storage, or re-lease to a different kind of tenant. A legal nonconforming use can continue but may not be enlarged or re-established after a lapse. Get the zoning designation and a written answer from the municipality about the uses you actually plan.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: What should I know about flood and stormwater for Chicago-area industrial sites?
t: Check the FEMA flood map first, then the local stormwater rules: in Cook County the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District administers a watershed management ordinance, and the collar counties and municipalities have their own requirements. Detention obligations can affect expansion plans and yard surfacing, and a flat, paved industrial site is not immune to drainage problems.

t: Will my purchase trigger a reassessment, and how do I underwrite it? In Illinois a recorded sale is evidence an assessor can use, and reassessment cycles differ: Cook County reassesses by region on a triennial cycle; the collar counties revalue on their own cycles with annual equalization. Underwrite the bill you are likely to pay after the sale, not the seller’s current bill, and confirm the leases let you recover increases. Build an appeal calendar during diligence. The property tax guide explains the process and links all nine county assessment offices. Does a Cook County Class 6b incentive stay with the property when it sells? Do not assume it. p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
t: How do lenders size loans on small industrial buildings, and what trips borrowers up? Lenders generally test loan-to-value, debt service coverage, and often debt yield, using their own definitions of income and expenses. What trips borrowers up is lease term shorter than loan term (expect rollover reserves or structure), environmental findings, appraisal gaps, recourse requirements, and prepayment terms that limit a later sale or refinance. Confirm definitions early and model the lender’s case, not just yours. The debt-service calculator shows the arithmetic. How should I think about refinancing risk at loan maturity? Assume the refinance happens at a higher rate, a lower loan amount, and a tougher appraisal than today, and see whether the property still carries itself. Moderate leverage, staggered maturities across a portfolio, extension options, and a capital plan that does not depend on cash-out proceeds are the usual defenses. When does SBA 504 financing matter to an investor? It matters because owner-users compete for the same buildings. A company planning to occupy most of a building can often finance it through the SBA 504 program with a long-term fixed-rate component, which lets it pay a price an investor cannot justify on rent alone. Expect that competition on vacant or soon-to-be-vacant buildings, and expect it to disappear on buildings with long leases in place.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
t: How do I decide between selling, refinancing, and holding? Start with capital: upcoming rollover, roof or pavement spending, loan maturity, tax basis and any exchange plan, and your own liquidity. Then ask whether you would buy the building today at the price you could sell it for. If the answer is no, the market is telling you something about the hold. The selling guide covers what buyers will ask for and how a sale actually runs. Who is the likely buyer of my building at exit? For 10,000 to 100,000 SF industrial, usually some mix of owner-users, private investors, exchange buyers, and smaller funds. The building’s size, condition, and lease profile decide which. A vacant functional building draws owner-users; a leased one with term draws investors and exchange buyers. Prepare the document file for the buyer you expect. How are off-market deals really sourced? Through relationships and persistence: direct outreach to owners, broker networks, estates and partnerships in transition, and lease expirations that make an owner rethink. Be fundable and fast when one arrives, and remember that “off-market” can mean mispriced in either direction. Underwrite it like any other deal.

p: Industrial building types and specifications
t: Industrial guide · Building function and specifications Industrial building types and specifications This guide explains common industrial building types and the physical specifications buyers, tenants, lenders, and advisors review for 10,000 to 100,000 square foot assets in Chicagoland. Educational, not an engineering report or valuation. Talk about your building Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap. Call (630) 570-2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com In brief Industrial labels are shorthand; the actual utility comes from loading, clear height, power, truck movement, fire protection, and zoning. A building can be excellent for one user and inefficient for another because operations, storage profile, labor, and equipment differ. p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Why type and spec matter for 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings
t: In the 10,000 to 100,000 square foot range, many assets are bought by owner-users, private investors, and local or regional tenants. The same building may be evaluated as an operating facility, an income investment, or a future re-tenanting opportunity. Owner-users often start with fit: doors, power, production flow, office area, parking, and expansion room. Tenants compare total occupancy cost, timing, lease obligations, and whether the site can support their operations without major disruption. Investors review the current lease profile and then ask who else could use the building if the tenant leaves. That is why the industrial building evaluation checklist and the seller file described in the selling guide focus on function, records, and verifiable facts. Function: Does the building support the use without unusual workarounds? Flexibility: Could another user occupy it if the first plan changes? Risk: Are there physical, zoning, environmental, or utility constraints that affect timing or cost?

p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Specifications explained and why each matters
t: A useful spec sheet explains both the number and the practical effect. Where possible, separate measured facts from assumptions or broker shorthand. Clear height Clear height is commonly measured from the finished floor to the lowest obstruction, not simply to the roof deck. It affects racking, equipment, lighting, and sprinkler design, and it should be checked against beams, joists, ducts, heaters, fans, and sprinkler piping. Column spacing and speed bays Column spacing affects storage layout, forklift movement, production cells, and future demising. Speed bays near docks can provide staging depth for loading, but verify actual dimensions and obstructions. Dock-high doors and door ratio Dock-high loading supports trailer-height movement and can be critical for distribution. Door-to-area ratios are a concept for comparing loading intensity, but the right ratio depends on the operation, trailer dwell, staffing, and truck scheduling. Drive-in doors Drive-in doors allow vehicles, equipment, or vans to enter at grade. Verify clear opening, apron slope, door condition, security, and whether grade changes affect safe use. Dock levelers, seals, shelters, and bumpers These components affect safety, weather protection, product handling, and dock efficiency. Condition, capacity, controls, and maintenance records should be reviewed during physical diligence. Truck court depth and turning

p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Class A, B, and C as informal labels
t: Industrial class labels are market shorthand, not a single official standard. They can be useful only when tied to facts that can be inspected and documented. Informal ways people describe industrial building class Label Common description Caution Class A Newer or recently modernized building with stronger loading, height, systems, truck circulation, life-safety features, and institutional-quality records. A small Class A building may still be wrong for a user if doors, power, or zoning do not fit. Class B Functional building with some older features, moderate office finish, usable loading, and a condition profile that may require selective capital work. Class B can be a broad category, so list the actual strengths and weaknesses. Class C Older or more specialized building with lower clear height, limited loading, heavier deferred maintenance, or narrower reuse. Class C does not mean unusable; it means the buyer pool may be more specific and diligence may be more important.

p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: How specs translate to buyer and tenant pools
t: Specifications shape demand because they determine who can operate efficiently. A property with strong doors, turning, power, and fire protection may appeal to a broader distribution or manufacturing audience than one with the same square footage but limited utility. Functional obsolescence occurs when older features reduce usefulness compared with current operating needs. Examples include low clear height, shallow truck courts, insufficient power, limited parking, heavy office finish, difficult column spacing, or loading that does not match the building size. Investors consider re-tenanting risk by asking how many users can realistically occupy the space, how long improvements might take, and what capital would be needed. For income-property context, see the investment diligence guide and the commercial leasing guide . Broader pool: flexible layout, adequate power, code-compliant improvements, documented systems, and common loading patterns. Narrower pool: very specialized equipment, unusual floor plan, unresolved environmental history, nonconforming yard, or limited truck access. Seller takeaway: disclose constraints clearly and support strengths with records rather than adjectives.

p: Truck dimensions and turning paths
t: Industrial guide · Fleet and site fit Truck dimensions and turning paths Use these sourced examples to ask better questions about loading, gates, driveways, yards, and truck courts. p: Truck dimensions and turning paths
h: Turning circle, swept path, and offtracking
t: Turning circle diameter vs. radius Diameter spans a complete circle; radius is half that diameter only when both refer to the same circle and measurement convention. A curb-to-curb wheel path is not a wall-to-wall body envelope. Ask which reference point, steering lock, speed, and maneuver the supplier measured. Swept path and outer sweep A swept path is the area occupied by the vehicle through a specific maneuver. Its outer boundary must account for front corners, mirrors, body overhang, and trailer swing, not just a tire track. Offtracking Rear wheels and a trailer do not follow the tractor's front-wheel path in a low-speed turn; they commonly track inward. Trailer length, wheelbase, axle locations, articulation, steering, and approach angle change the path. Design vehicle AASHTO design-vehicle labels such as WB-62 and WB-67 describe particular geometric templates, not interchangeable fleet measurements or a universal radius. A qualified engineer must select a suitable current design vehicle and check it against the site's actual fleet and maneuvers. No numerical turning radius is supplied here because the cited fleet specifications do not establish one for a complete configuration. Forward circulation, reversing into a dock, simultaneous opposing traffic, and queuing require different checks. FHWA road-size limits are not turning-path templates.

Survey the constraints: gate openings, curb returns, driveways, dock angles, court depth, grade changes, fences, bollards, poles, parked vehicles, easements, fire access, snow storage, and overhead obstructions. Test the maneuver: have a qualified civil/transportation engineer perform fleet-specific swept-path analysis for entry, turns, backing, unloading, and exit, including required operational margins and conflicts. Check access and operation: local truck routes, bridge/underpass restrictions, delivery rules, pavement capacity, loading equipment, and municipal approvals. Legal road width or nominal cargo size is not a guaranteed safe clearance. p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Industrial property diligence is not limited to rent, taxes, and a walk-through. Past and current operations may involve chemicals, fuels, tanks, floor drains, heavy equipment, vehicle repair, food handling, manufacturing residues, or unusual utility loads. Physical systems also carry deal risk. A roof, slab, dock package, sprinkler system, transformer, truck court, or drainage problem can change occupancy timing and capital needs. For a broader acquisition framework, see the investment diligence guide . For building-fit questions, use the industrial evaluation checklist and the building types and specifications guide .

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: The purchase and sale agreement should state when the diligence period starts, what the seller must deliver, what access is allowed, and what happens if the buyer objects. Calendar every notice date before ordering reports. Access needs should be specific. Environmental consultants, roofers, surveyors, engineers, lenders, insurers, contractors, appraisers, and utility representatives may need different site visits, tenant coordination, and sampling permissions. Sellers can reduce friction by pre-assembling the documents listed in the selling guide . A clean file does not replace diligence, but it helps buyers and lenders ask better questions. Use a diligence tracker with document status, responsible party, deadline, and open issue. Require insurance, safety rules, and escort procedures for invasive or operationally sensitive inspections. Coordinate tenant notices and quiet-hours if the property is occupied. Reserve enough time for follow-up testing when the initial report identifies a concern.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: A recognized environmental condition, or REC, points to a likely presence or release of hazardous substances or petroleum products. A historical recognized environmental condition, or HREC, generally indicates a past release that has been addressed to the applicable standard. A controlled recognized environmental condition, or CREC, generally means a past release remains subject to controls, restrictions, or ongoing obligations. The words matter because they can affect lender review, buyer obligations, and future use.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Phase II sampling and vapor intrusion
t: A Phase II investigation may include soil, groundwater, soil-gas, indoor air, or other sampling. The purpose is to test specific concerns, not to prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property. Vapor intrusion review can be important where volatile chemicals or petroleum releases may migrate into buildings. Sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design should be handled by qualified environmental professionals.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Asbestos, lead, PCBs, USTs, and other regulated materials
t: Older industrial buildings may require separate review for asbestos-containing materials, lead-based paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground storage tanks, aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. These are often outside a basic Phase I scope unless specifically added. Ask whether the consultant recommends targeted surveys before demolition, renovation, financing, or occupancy. Removal and disposal rules can affect timing and cost.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Illinois EPA SRP and NFR letters
t: The Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program is a voluntary cleanup program that can lead to a No Further Remediation letter for addressed conditions. An NFR letter is not the same as saying every environmental risk is gone. Review the recorded terms, institutional controls, engineered barriers, exposure routes, and future-use limits. Counsel and the consultant should confirm whether the proposed use remains consistent with the closure.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Federal landowner liability protections are concept-based and fact-specific. They may depend on proper AAI, continuing obligations, no affiliation issues, and conduct after acquisition. Do not treat a report alone as a guarantee. Review the facts with environmental counsel before relying on any protection.

t: Pavement matters for trailers, forklifts, snow removal, drainage, and yard use. Inspect asphalt, concrete, catch basins, detention, ponding, striping, curbs, and truck-wear areas. Flood and drainage review should include local records and the FEMA Flood Map Service Center . FEMA mapping does not replace a civil engineer's review of site drainage or stormwater obligations.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Accessibility review should consider parking, routes, entrances, restrooms, office areas, signage, and any alterations. Elevators, hoists, cranes, bridge cranes, and jib cranes require records, load ratings, inspections, service contracts, and ownership clarification.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Title and survey review connects legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey helps show boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments. Review access rights, shared drive agreements, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage rights, recorded covenants, and any reciprocal easement agreements. A truck entrance that crosses another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use. For rail-served property, confirm rail agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and whether the railroad or a third party controls access. Rail value can disappear if the legal and physical service rights do not match the marketing description.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Zoning diligence should confirm the current district, permitted uses, special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours of operation. A zoning verification letter can help document how the municipality views the property. Permits and certificates of occupancy show whether past work and uses were approved. Check for open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements that may need closeout. For local research starting points, use the nine-county hub and municipal records. For Chicago-specific research, see the Chicago commercial real estate guide .

h: Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial
t: Lease diligence should test whether the income, obligations, and operational rights shown in the rent roll are supported by signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and notice relevant to occupancy. Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims. SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change. CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances. Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements. Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports. Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles. The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
t: Industrial users often need utility confirmation before they can commit. Electricity, gas, water, sanitary sewer, storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom should be reviewed against the user's equipment and occupancy schedule. For much of the region, electrical capacity questions may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the tenant's equipment vendor. Confirm service voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements. Gas, water, and sewer review should include meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. Fiber and telecom are separate from an address being generally serviceable.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Turning findings into price, credits, escrows, or repairs
t: Diligence findings are useful only when they lead to a clear decision. The buyer can accept the risk, renegotiate price, request a credit, create an escrow, require seller repairs, modify representations, obtain insurance, or terminate if the contract allows. Sellers should distinguish between documented defects, buyer preferences, and speculative future upgrades. Buyers should distinguish between ordinary maintenance and issues that change value, financing, insurability, or lawful use. Material findings should be tied to evidence: report page, photo, contractor proposal, municipal response, title exception, lease clause, or consultant memo. That keeps negotiations focused on facts.

h: How Illinois property tax works at a high level
t: Industrial property taxes in Illinois are local taxes administered through a state-supervised system. The short version is assessment, equalization, levy, rate, bill, and collection. Each step should be checked against the parcel’s county, municipality, school district, and special districts. From assessment to bill Assessment The assessor estimates taxable value. Outside Cook County, Illinois generally uses a statutory assessment level of 33⅓% of fair cash value before equalization and exemptions. Cook County applies its own classification levels. Equalization An equalization factor, also called a multiplier, may adjust assessments so assessment levels are more uniform. See assessed value and equalization factor . Levy Taxing districts adopt levies for schools, municipalities, counties, parks, libraries, fire, sanitary, and other local services. Rate and extension The county clerk extends rates against equalized assessed value. The rate is not set by the assessor. Bill and collection The county treasurer sends and collects the bill. Illinois property taxes are commonly paid after the tax year and in installments; confirm the exact calendar with the county treasurer.
